result: Two rhesus monkeys were surgically implanted with recording chambers over the left supplementary motor area (SMA), guided by structural MRI. Neural recordings were performed using seven independent movable microelectrodes across 131 experimental sessions, with spikes sampled at 30 KHz and local field potentials (LFPs) filtered at 0.5-500 Hz and sampled at 2 KHz.
evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C23, and C135-C139 provide comprehensive methodological details about subjects, surgical procedures, recording locations, and data acquisition parameters. These are standard neuroscience methods that are well-documented and internally consistent.

result: Monkeys successfully performed a visual metronome task in which they maintained internal rhythms (500, 750, or 1000 ms intervals) in the absence of sensory stimuli and overt motor commands. Performance exceeded 80% correct (94±0.2% monkey 1; 86±0.3% monkey 2) but declined as a function of elapsed time, consistent with Weber's Law of timing and scalar variability.
evaluation: Claims C5-C15 and C22 describe the behavioral task and performance with quantitative data (n=131 sessions). The decline in performance is well-characterized and fits established timing models. The task design successfully dissociates rhythm maintenance from motor execution.

result: Behavioral performance at the 4th maintenance interval for 750 and 1000 ms tempos was higher than expected from the timing model, possibly because monkeys exploited knowledge that the experiment included only up to four maintenance intervals.
evaluation: Claims C16-C17 identify a deviation from the model but offer only speculative explanation. While the observation is data-driven, the interpretation lacks experimental validation. The authors acknowledge this as speculation and suggest future experimental modifications.

result: Reaction times to the go-cue increased significantly with elapsed time (slope=11 ms/s, p<0.001, R²=0.72), potentially reflecting increasing difficulty in estimating stimulus position. Larger gamma band amplitudes correlated with increased reaction times, and gamma activity decreased at movement onset, replaced by low-frequency oscillations.
evaluation: Claims C18-C21 provide quantitative analysis with statistical support and references to supplementary figures. The correlation between gamma amplitude and reaction time is documented, and the movement-related changes in oscillatory activity are consistent with prior literature.

result: LFP power in the 30-40 Hz gamma band was up to two-fold larger than baseline (p<0.001, permutation test) and exhibited rhythmic structure that increased at stimulus transitions and as a function of total elapsed time. This pattern was consistent across all three interval durations (500, 750, 1000 ms).
evaluation: Claims C24-C27, C32, C140-C141 describe gamma band modulations with appropriate statistical testing and methodological details. The spectral analysis methods (multitaper with 200 ms windows) are standard and well-cited. The consistency across tempos strengthens the finding.

result: Single-trial LFP recordings revealed transient gamma bursts (defined as periods exceeding the 90th percentile for ≥100 ms) that coincided with times when the stimulus would have switched positions during maintenance intervals. Mean gamma amplitude at switch times was significantly higher than at mid-interval (p<0.01, t-test).
evaluation: Claims C28-C31 and C142 describe single-trial burst analysis with clear operational definitions and statistical validation. The temporal alignment between bursts and task structure is demonstrated both qualitatively (figures) and quantitatively (statistical tests).

result: During maintenance intervals, there were no motor actions or periodic visual stimuli—only the tempo of the internal rhythm differed between trial types. LFPs in SMA encoded internal rhythms through gamma bursts synchronized with the beats of the previously presented visual metronome, with burst amplitude providing a neural correlate for total elapsed time.
evaluation: Claims C33-C35, C38-C39 establish the key interpretation that gamma bursts reflect internally maintained rhythms rather than sensory or motor processes. The experimental design (absence of stimuli/movement during maintenance) supports this conclusion, though alternative interpretations are addressed in later control experiments.

result: Gamma bursts had similar temporal profiles across tempos and intervals when aligned to onset. Burst amplitude increased exponentially with elapsed time during maintenance intervals (R²=0.86) and linearly during entrainment intervals (R²=0.94).
evaluation: Claims C36-C37 and C73 provide quantitative characterization of burst properties with high model fits. The temporal scaling across different interval durations demonstrates that the neural mechanism adapts to different tempos while maintaining consistent burst structure.

result: Error trials showed systematic deviations: on fast tempo trials (500 ms), gamma oscillated at slower frequencies (right-shifted dynamics), while on slow tempo trials (1000 ms), gamma oscillated at faster frequencies (left-shifted dynamics). This pattern indicates monkeys lagged behind fast tempos and got ahead of slow ones, consistent with previous findings in humans and confirmed by behavioral data from a six-choice task variant.
evaluation: Claims C40-C46, C50, C113, C116-C117, C119-C120 provide converging evidence from spectral analysis, behavioral patterns, and cross-validation with a six-choice task. The systematic nature of errors (not random) and consistency with prior human studies strengthen the interpretation.

result: A logistic classifier could differentiate correct from error trials with increasing accuracy as a function of elapsed time, demonstrating that the internal rhythm progressively fell out of sync with the correct tempo. Classification accuracy was cross-validated on held-out trials (50 correct, 50 error).
evaluation: Claims C47-C49, C143-C144 describe a machine learning analysis with appropriate cross-validation. The increasing classification accuracy over time provides quantitative support for the drift hypothesis and complements the spectral analyses.

result: Mean error activity represents a mixture of lagging and leading tempos and does not necessarily reflect the half-cycle desynchronization underlying individual incorrect responses.
evaluation: Claims C51-C52 provide important caveats about interpreting averaged error data. This acknowledgment of heterogeneity in error types demonstrates appropriate caution in interpretation and is supported by reference to supplementary data.

result: In a delayed-reach control task with exponentially distributed delays (1100-3000 ms, flat hazard rate), SMA generated gamma bursts that increased in frequency and amplitude during motor preparation. These findings are consistent with gamma bursts encoding impending motor commands and support the interpretation that rhythmic gamma in the metronome task reflects alternating motor plans.
evaluation: Claims C53-C59, C101-C102 describe a well-designed control experiment that addresses the motor preparation hypothesis. The use of an exponential distribution (flat hazard rate) controls for temporal expectation effects, strengthening the interpretation that gamma reflects motor planning.

result: During entrainment intervals (where no motor response was required), gamma bursts were present and increased in amplitude after each stimulus, but peaked after stimulus presentation rather than at switches. Gamma dynamics differed across consecutive intervals and tempos (p<0.01, chi-squared tests), with responses similar only during the first 500 ms when tempo information was unavailable. The amplitude drop 500 ms after the third interval suggests gamma encodes cognitive knowledge about task structure, not purely sensory responses.
evaluation: Claims C60-C72 provide multiple lines of evidence against a pure sensory interpretation: (1) phase differences between entrainment and maintenance, (2) statistical differences across intervals/tempos, (3) task-structure-dependent amplitude changes. The chi-squared tests with multiple comparison corrections support the statistical claims.

result: The SMA circuit reflected both periodic interval timing (through burst timing) and total elapsed time (through burst amplitude) during entrainment.
evaluation: Claim C74 synthesizes findings about dual encoding of interval and cumulative time. This is supported by the quantitative analyses in C37 and C73 showing different relationships between amplitude and time during different task epochs.

result: Single-unit recordings from 113 SMA neurons showed firing patterns that resembled gamma-band LFP modulations: oscillatory amplitude modulations during entrainment and maintenance, increases with elapsed time, and preparatory activity in the delayed-reach task. Neurons exhibited spatial preferences (74 preferred right, 39 preferred left), determined by cross-correlation between stimulus position and firing rate.
evaluation: Claims C75-C81 and C145 describe single-unit analyses that parallel LFP findings. The spatial preference analysis is methodologically sound, and the consistency between spiking and LFP patterns strengthens the overall interpretation of SMA's role in rhythm maintenance.

result: Cross-correlation analysis of firing rates between correct and error trials independently corroborated that errors resulted from the internal metronome lagging behind fast rhythms (500, 750 ms: negative lag peaks) and getting ahead of slow rhythms (1000 ms: positive lag peak).
evaluation: Claims C82-C84 and C118 provide independent validation of the error pattern using single-unit data. The cross-correlation approach complements the LFP spectral analyses and strengthens confidence in the interpretation of systematic timing errors.

result: Spike-triggered average (STA) analysis revealed that LFP activity recorded simultaneously with spikes had a power peak at 30 Hz, especially during maintenance intervals (factorial ANOVA: p<0.05). The spike-gamma association was stronger at stimulus transitions (t-test p<0.005), and jittering spike times by ±15 ms eliminated the gamma peak, demonstrating temporal specificity. These results suggest gamma oscillations help synchronize neuronal firing for more effective downstream communication.
evaluation: Claims C85-C89, C146-C147 describe spike-field coupling analysis with appropriate statistical tests and controls (jitter analysis). The methods are standard and well-cited. The interpretation about synchronization is appropriately framed as consistent with prior literature rather than definitively proven.

result: LFP coherence between simultaneously recorded electrodes decayed as a function of distance (R²=0.72), demonstrating that recorded signals reflect local neuronal circuits rather than volume conduction from distant sources.
evaluation: Claims C90-C91 and C148 address an important methodological concern about signal source. The coherence analysis with clear distance-dependent decay provides strong evidence for local generation of the LFP signals. The method is well-defined and appropriately applied.

result: Monkeys can maintain rhythms without sensory stimuli or overt motor commands. Internal rhythms are encoded by gamma-band LFP bursts in SMA, with burst timing indicating rhythm intervals and amplitude indicating total elapsed time. Single-neuron spikes are associated with gamma-band LFP, consistent with gamma facilitating neuronal synchronization for enhanced postsynaptic impact.
evaluation: Claims C92-C95, C122-C123 summarize the main findings. These conclusions are well-supported by the convergent evidence from behavioral performance, LFP dynamics, single-unit recordings, and spike-field coupling. The interpretation about dual encoding (interval and cumulative time) is directly supported by quantitative analyses.

result: The metronome task involves rhythmic modulation in motor response likelihood, which could relate to periodic gamma bursts and firing rates. However, rhythmicity is also observed during entrainment intervals where no movement is required. The increasing hazard rate (go-cue probability) could explain amplitude increases, though the delayed-reach control with flat hazard rate also showed amplitude increases.
evaluation: Claims C96-C100 present alternative interpretations related to motor preparation and temporal expectation. The authors appropriately note that rhythmicity during entrainment (C98) argues against pure motor preparation, and the control task results (C102) argue against hazard rate as the sole explanation. These remain partially unresolved alternative hypotheses.

result: The authors favor the interpretation that SMA participates in the metronome task by generating a dynamic motor plan that matches the spatio-temporal tempo of the rhythmic visual stimulus. The internal metronome is encoded as a dynamic motor plan initiated during entrainment, with tempo encoded by burst timing (not amplitude).
evaluation: Claims C103, C111-C112 present the authors' preferred mechanistic interpretation. This is supported by the delayed-reach control experiment, the presence of activity during entrainment, and the spatial preferences of neurons. The clarification that tempo is encoded by timing rather than amplitude (C112) is important and well-supported.

result: SMA plays a central role in motor planning and execution, is anatomically connected to M1, parietal and frontal lobes, and brainstem motor nuclei, and shows activity correlating with motor, cognitive, emotional, and perceptual functions. SMA is active before movement, participating in action selection and timing. In the current study, SMA activity began during entrainment, seconds before movement was required, consistent with preparatory activity as the initial state of a dynamical system for movement control.
evaluation: Claims C104-C110 provide context from prior literature (well-cited) and connect it to current findings. The observation that activity begins during entrainment (C110) is data-driven and supports the interpretation within the dynamical systems framework.

result: Even on error trials, gamma activity and neuronal firing show rhythmic dynamics and amplitude increases with elapsed time, with three independent lines of evidence supporting that errors arise from desynchronization of the internal metronome.
evaluation: Claims C114-C115 introduce the synthesis of error-related findings. The three lines of evidence (spectral analysis, cross-correlations, six-choice behavioral data) are detailed in other claim groups and provide strong converging support.

result: The current results address the debate about whether rhythmic tasks rely on measuring individual intervals versus total elapsed time, showing that both are encoded (rhythmic activity for intervals, amplitude for cumulative time). The findings extend previous work on temporal scaling in single neurons to LFP oscillations and fit within an emerging framework where time-estimation signals are distributed across motor structures as dynamic motor plans.
evaluation: Claims C121-C134 contextualize findings within the broader timing literature. The citations are appropriate and the connections to prior work (particularly Wang et al., 2018 on temporal scaling) are well-justified. The extension from single-unit to LFP dynamics (C133) is a novel contribution supported by the data.
